standard.title: Question, compare and discuss ideas
standard.description: use the target language in exchanges to question, offer opinions and compare and discuss ideas
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain interactions to exchange personal opinions and experiences (AC9LS10EC01) and can express basic opinions using set phrases (AC9LS8EC02). They have not yet participated in structured discussion or debate where they question others' views, compare arguments and develop position-based exchanges.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students use the target language to participate in exchanges involving questioning, expressing and justifying opinions, and comparing and discussing ideas — including on topics of current or social relevance.

nodes.label: Questioning and probing ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use the target language to ask questions that probe, clarify or challenge an idea or opinion expressed by another.
nodes.minimum_width: Ask at least two follow-up or probing questions in the target language in response to a partner's expressed opinion.
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of questioning strategies to probe, clarify and explore ideas; ask for evidence, examples or elaboration; use questions to steer or deepen a discussion.
wider: Use Socratic questioning techniques in the target language — practise probing without asserting, letting questions guide the reasoning
Analyse how questioning strategies differ in formal debate vs informal discussion in the target language — identify conventions specific to each

response_modes.reason: Probing questions require a bank of question forms beyond simple information requests. Students need exposure to a range of probing question types (why, what evidence, what if, can you give an example) in varied discussion contexts before applying them spontaneously.

success_criteria: Asks at least two questions that probe or extend a partner's opinion (not just factual information questions)
Can distinguish between a clarifying question and a challenging question in the target language

nodes.label: Offering and justifying opinions in discussion
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can express and justify opinions on topics of current or social interest in the target language, using appropriate discussion language.
nodes.minimum_width: Express and briefly justify at least one opinion on a current or social topic in the target language, using at least one justification structure.
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of structures to express, justify and nuance opinions; identify pros, cons and limitations of ideas; use persuasion language and slogans or rhetorical devices where appropriate.
wider: Participate in a structured class debate on a current issue in the target language — argue an assigned position and respond to counter-arguments
Compose a short opinion text (letter, post, spoken statement) for a real or simulated audience on a topic of personal or social relevance
nodes.hinge_reason: Justified opinion expression is the communicative core of EC02. Students who can only assert ('I think it's good') without justification ('because...', 'however...', 'this shows that...') cannot participate meaningfully in discussion or debate. This also underpins EC06's persuasive text creation.

response_modes.reason: Justified opinions require explicit reasoning scaffolds — students need modelled examples of how justification structures work in the target language before they can deploy them independently. Structured debate and opinion frames provide the scaffold.
Opinion expression should be practised across a range of topics so that the structures transfer beyond one familiar topic area.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Participating in discussion and debate on topics of current social relevance is where language learning becomes genuinely purposeful. Students develop argumentation skills in the target language that have direct real-world application.
success_criteria: Expresses an opinion with at least one justification in the target language
Can identify and respond to a counter-argument rather than simply restating their original position

nodes.label: Comparing and evaluating ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare ideas, weigh perspectives and discuss implications in the target language, moving beyond assertion to evaluation.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare at least two perspectives on a topic in the target language; identify at least one strength and one limitation of a position.
nodes.typical_width: Compare and evaluate ideas across multiple perspectives; distinguish between fact and opinion; identify shared and divergent values underlying different positions; use comparison and evaluation language structures.
wider: Analyse a persuasive text in the target language — identify the rhetorical strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness
Compare media representations of the same topic across target language and Australian English sources — identify where framing differs and discuss why

response_modes.reason: Comparing and evaluating ideas integrates questioning (node 1) and justified opinion expression (node 2) into the full discussion capacity the descriptor demands. Tasks that require students to represent and evaluate multiple perspectives simultaneously are the key integration structure.

success_criteria: Can compare at least two perspectives on a topic and identify a strength and limitation of each
Uses comparison language structures in the target language accurately enough for the comparison to be clear
